identity.stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with proximal leg weakness that improves after climbing a few flights of stairs. She also reports dry mouth. Examination reveals decreased reflexes that improve after repeated muscle contraction. What is the most likely diagnosis?

sources: MedCORE-6716-MCQs.txt rich duplicate [2164] for the identical stem; mapped its explanations to MEDCNS02's reordered options by option text.

layers.hook: Exercise improves the weakness + dry mouth + postexercise reflex facilitation → LEMS, not MG.
layers.trap: Both LEMS and myasthenia gravis can cause proximal weakness. Here, improvement after repeated contraction plus dry mouth and reflex facilitation are the discriminators for LEMS.
layers.rule: LEMS is a presynaptic neuromuscular-junction disorder, commonly associated with antibodies to P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels that reduce acetylcholine release. Its typical pattern is proximal weakness with autonomic symptoms and reduced reflexes; brief exercise may transiently facilitate strength and reflexes.

others.A: Myasthenia gravis typically causes fatigable weakness that worsens with repeated use and improves with rest; the exercise-related facilitation and dry mouth in this stem favor LEMS.
others.C: Guillain–Barré syndrome usually causes progressive ascending weakness with reduced or absent reflexes, not the postexercise facilitation and autonomic pattern described here.
others.D: Polymyositis can cause proximal weakness, but it does not explain the characteristic postexercise facilitation and autonomic symptoms in this stem.

identity.stem: A girl of six years experiences moments of gazing and non-communication, with her EEG revealing 3/sec, synchronized spike-wave discharges. Which anti-epileptic drug is most suitable for her?

sources: Past Papers/Past Papers - Full/Aug 2023.rtf: explanation for the 3-Hz spike-and-wave/ethosuximide pairing.

layers.hook: Six-year-old + brief staring + 3-Hz spike-wave → childhood absence → ethosuximide.
layers.trap: Do not choose an antiseizure drug by name alone: the 3-Hz generalized spike-wave pattern identifies typical childhood absence, for which ethosuximide is the preferred initial treatment when absence is the only seizure type.
layers.rule: The age, brief staring episodes, and synchronous 3-Hz spike-and-wave EEG are characteristic of childhood absence epilepsy. Ethosuximide is the preferred initial monotherapy when seizures are absence-only; it blocks low-threshold T-type calcium currents in thalamic neurons involved in the synchronized spike-wave rhythm.

others.A: Phenytoin may aggravate typical absence seizures and should not be chosen for this presentation.
others.B: Gabapentin is not effective for childhood absence seizures.
others.C: Primidone is not a recommended initial monotherapy for childhood absence epilepsy; ethosuximide is the preferred first choice for absence-only disease.
